blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an array `nums` of size `n`, return the **majority element** — the value that appears **more than n / 2 times**. You may assume a majority element always exists.

blocks.alt: The array [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]. The four 2s are highlighted: 2 appears 4 times out of 7, which is more than half.

elements.text: 2 appears 4 times, n / 2 = 3.5  →  2 is the majority
elements.originalText: 2 appears 4 times, n / 2 = 3.5  →  2 is the majority

blocks.text: Example

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [3, 2, 3]
Output: 3

Input:  nums = [2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2]
Output: 2

blocks.text: Understanding the problem
"More than half" is a strong promise. It means the majority value outnumbers **all the other values put together**. Keep that sentence in mind — the clever solution is built entirely on it.
Approach 1: count with a hash map
Count how often each value appears, and return the one whose count passes `n / 2`.

Straightforward and **O(n)** time, but the map can hold up to n/2 different values: **O(n) extra space**. (Sorting and taking the middle element also works — the majority must cover the middle — but costs O(n log n).)
The key insight: let the values cancel each other out

Imagine every element is a voter. Pair up two **different** values and remove them both — one majority vote and one other vote cancel. Because the majority has more votes than everyone else combined, it can never be cancelled completely: whatever survives at the end must be the majority.

blocks.alt: Pairing different values: each 1 is paired with a 2 and both are crossed out. One 2 is left over, so 2 is the majority.

elements.text: … and a 2 is still left over
elements.originalText: … and a 2 is still left over

blocks.text: Boyer–Moore voting algorithm
We can do the cancelling in a single pass with just two variables: a `candidate` and its `count`.

items: If `count` is 0, nobody is ahead — the current value becomes the new `candidate`.
If the current value equals the candidate, `count` goes up by one (a supporting vote).
Otherwise `count` goes down by one (a vote cancelled).

blocks.text: Dry run it yourself
Try `[1, 3, 3, 2, 3, 3, 3]`, where the majority only takes over late. If you enter an array with **no** majority, the simulator will show why the problem's guarantee matters.

Complexity

blocks.alt: Hash map counting: O(n) time and O(n) space. Boyer–Moore voting: O(n) time and O(1) space.

blocks.text: One pass and two variables: **O(n) time, O(1) space**.
Edge cases to test

items: **If a majority isn't guaranteed**, count the final candidate in a second pass and only return it if it really appears more than n / 2 times.

blocks.text: Where this idea shows up again

The follow-up "find every value that appears more than **n / 3** times" uses the same cancelling idea with **two** candidates and two counts — at most two values can pass n / 3. More broadly, "let opposing items cancel" is a neat trick for any problem where one group is guaranteed to outnumber the rest.
